items.quote: The whole kiss-and-tell thing is a negative approach that often happens in a World Cup. We will see negative stories about the players and it can affect their confidence and the overall performance of the national team on the pitch, let alone the bid to actually stage the competition.
items.author: Gary Lineker

items.title: A team of Gemini 4 Argon agents beats Minecraft
items.abstract: This paper demonstrates the first end-to-end autonomous completion of Minecraft's survival mode by AI agents. Four Gemini 4 Argon agents, coordinating via chat and shared memory, independently planned, wrote, and debugged all necessary programs to defeat the Ender Dragon, showcasing emergent complex behavior from a simple goal.
items.figure_caption: The four agents, and their run step by step: the thirteen steps from bare hands to the Ender Dragon, each colored by the player who reached it first, over 27 hours and 14 minutes. Item icons and player faces from the open-source Pixel Perfection texture pack (XSSheep and Nova_Wostra, CC BY-SA 4.0), not Minecraft’s textures.

items.title: AutoSFT: An Agentic System for Automated Data Research in Supervised Fine-Tuning
items.abstract: This paper introduces AutoSFT, a multi-agent system designed to automate supervised fine-tuning data research. Unlike previous methods that offer limited control, AutoSFT employs a meta-agent to manage analysis and execution, and sub-agents to perform a comprehensive range of data manipulation tasks. This approach allows for more sophisticated data refinement, including pruning, repairing, and synthesizing data, leading to improved model performance.
items.figure_caption: Overview of AutoSFT. The meta agent commits a recipe. An executor trains and evaluates it separately and returns artifact paths. Analysis subagents read these artifacts from complementary angles, and a synthesis subagent writes data for undersupplied capabilities. The meta agent integrates their proposals into the next recipe. All roles share a candidate data pool and a skill library.

items.title: Designing Transformers for Continuous Diffusion Language Models
items.abstract: This paper addresses the suboptimal Transformer architectures used in continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs). It introduces LangDiT, a novel architecture incorporating specific normalization, conditioning, and training techniques tailored for CDLMs. LangDiT significantly improves generation perplexity, setting a new state-of-the-art for continuous language generation.

items.title: Learning to Steer LLM Agents and Multi-Agent Systems
items.abstract: This paper introduces a "steering agent" designed to prevent goal drift in LLM agents and multi-agent systems. The steering agent monitors execution in real-time, using a fast path to detect drift and a slow path to correct it. By jointly training these paths with reinforcement learning, the system learns to effectively supervise and guide LLM agents towards their intended goals.

items.title: LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents
items.abstract: LEASH addresses the challenge of efficiently using powerful AI agents for long-horizon tasks by intelligently escalating control from a cheaper, weaker agent to a more capable, stronger agent. Its core method involves a multi-layered uncertainty estimation system that triggers escalation when needed and then monitors the strong agent's actions to ensure it stays on track. This framework's contribution is a training-free approach that significantly reduces computational costs while maintaining performance by providing adaptive oversight.

items.title: Librarian Agents: Training LLMs to Curate Long-Context Workspaces that Anticipate Future Queries
items.abstract: This paper introduces Librarian Agents, a novel framework that trains LLMs to proactively curate long-context workspaces. Instead of reactive retrieval, these agents learn to reorganize unstructured documents into a hierarchical filesystem with synthetic files and links. This anticipatory curation aims to efficiently serve diverse future queries by creating optimized, reusable workspaces.
items.figure_caption: Overview of Librarian Agents. (Left) We train a builder agent to construct a workspace consisting of synthetic files and directories that anticipates future queries for a downstream answering agent. (Right) This workspace is built once and repeatedly used to answer different queries.

items.title: MLExpert: Towards a Generalist Agentic Model for Autonomous Machine Learning Engineering
items.abstract: This paper introduces MLExpert, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model designed for autonomous machine learning engineering. Its core method is a post-training approach that enables long-horizon optimization by effectively selecting useful supervision from lengthy experimental trajectories and learning from intermediate outcomes. MLExpert contributes a practical pathway towards AI for AI and recursive self-improvement by autonomously managing and optimizing complex ML engineering workflows.
items.figure_caption: Decision making in long-horizon MLE optimization. (a) External orchestration organizes optimization through predefined workflows and search rules. (b) In model-directed interaction, the model selects subsequent actions based on experimental states and execution feedback.

items.title: Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Mosaic addresses the limitations of single-session reinforcement learning by introducing a multi-session framework. Its core method, critic-free hierarchical optimization, estimates trajectory-level advantages by incorporating session-usage signals and guides session allocation within trajectories, improving agent performance across multiple interaction sessions.
items.figure_caption: The comparison between multi-session and single-session trajectories.

items.title: Terminal-RSI: Recursive Self-Improving Terminal Agents via Recursive Self-Rewrite and Policy-Refine
items.abstract: Terminal-RSI is a method for improving terminal agents by recursively rewriting verified trajectories and refining policies. It uses novel reward functions (FDR, SPR) and a turn-aware baseline (TB-GAE) to effectively leverage partial progress and verifier feedback. This recursive self-improvement process leads to significant performance gains on various terminal task benchmarks.

items.title: CAT-alyzing Honesty: Continuous Adversarial Training for Transferable LLM Honesty
items.abstract: This paper introduces Continuous Adversarial Training for Consistent Honesty (CATCH), a method to improve LLM honesty. CATCH trains models to produce honest answers while simultaneously avoiding dishonest ones, even when faced with pressure or specific scenarios. The contribution lies in demonstrating that CATCH effectively and transferably reduces LLM dishonesty across various benchmarks with minimal training data.

items.title: AI Consilium: a Benchmark of LLM Clinical Multidisciplinary Second Opinions
items.abstract: This paper introduces AI Consilium, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs' ability to provide multidisciplinary clinical second opinions. The core method involves using physician-calibrated LLM judges to assess LLM-generated reports on complex medical cases, focusing on factual grounding, clinical coherence, actionability, and safety. The contribution lies in demonstrating that LLMs can generate useful clinical second opinions, with structured outputs generally leading to higher quality, particularly in management recommendations.

items.title: Believed but Not Said: Measuring Hidden Belief Collapse in Multi-Agent LLM Discussions
items.abstract: This paper investigates how adversarial agents can manipulate multi-agent LLM discussions. The core method involves introducing a small number of agents asserting false information and then measuring how benign agents' private beliefs and public stances change. The key contribution is demonstrating that LLM groups are susceptible to belief collapse, with benign agents often privately adopting false beliefs without publicly endorsing them, a phenomenon termed "hidden belief collapse."
items.figure_caption: Overview. Ten agents discuss one fact for 16 rounds with k ∈ { 0 , 1 , 3 } k\( \in \)\{0,1,3\} adversarial agents pushing a false claim. Each round we measure both a benign agent’s public utterance and a private probe.

items.title: CART: Compatible Routing for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
items.abstract: This paper addresses catastrophic forgetting in multimodal instruction tuning by proposing Compatible Routing (CART). CART explicitly coordinates the adaptation of the visual projector and the language model by using task-specific experts for both modules. This joint adaptation, through weighted mixtures and inferred weights, aims to reduce representation drift and improve continual learning performance.

items.title: Disagreement-Guided Weak-to-Strong Routing
items.abstract: This paper proposes a novel method for "Disagreement-Guided Weak-to-Strong Routing" that avoids the need for costly ground-truth supervision. The core idea is to route a weak model's response to a stronger model based on the disagreement between multiple responses generated by the weak model itself. This disagreement signal serves as a proxy for correctness, enabling more efficient and reliable deployment of smaller models in resource-constrained environments.
items.figure_caption: Corrected disagreement better approximates optimal routing than alternatives.

items.title: Explaining the Roles of Experts in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs for Personalization
items.abstract: This paper proposes personalizing Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs to address the challenges of understanding and controlling personalization in user-centric applications. By adapting MoE models and training crosscoders on their activations, the authors identify specific experts responsible for distinct personalization features. This approach enables more interpretable and localized personalization compared to dense LLMs, while maintaining competitive performance and reducing polysemanticity.

items.title: Improving Environment-Agnostic Coding Agents: The Role of Scaffolding
items.abstract: This paper investigates how to improve environment-agnostic coding agents without environment-specific engineering. The core method involves modifying agent instructions to encourage reporting difficulties and enabling automatic continuation, which demonstrably improves performance on some benchmarks. The contribution lies in showing that even with advanced models, strategic scaffolding focused on agent control and organization, rather than explicit knowledge, remains crucial for enhancing performance.

items.title: OS-Helix: Unifying GUI Interaction and Code Execution in Native Computer-Using Agents
items.abstract: OS-Helix is a multimodal agent that unifies GUI interaction and code execution by training end-to-end on hybrid data. Its core method involves creating realistic, executable desktop environments and generating grounded tasks to teach the agent how to seamlessly switch between visual and programmatic actions. This approach overcomes limitations of prompt-level tool composition, enabling more effective native computer-using agents.
items.figure_caption: Overview of GUI-only, code-only, and hybrid computer use.

items.title: PROBE: Learning to Audit Policy Compliance in Tool-Using LLM Agents
items.abstract: This paper introduces PROBE, a method for training LLM-based auditors to detect policy violations in tool-using LLM agents. PROBE works by simulating realistic user interactions to uncover subtle, multi-turn policy breaches that traditional evaluation methods miss. Its core contribution is a novel approach to auditing agent compliance beyond just task completion or safety.

items.title: Realtime-Bench: Can Frontier Models Solve Real-time Interactive Problems?
items.abstract: This paper introduces Realtime-Bench, a new benchmark for evaluating large language models' ability to act in real-time interactive environments with strict temporal constraints. The benchmark reveals that current frontier models struggle significantly with these challenges, achieving low success rates even under ideal conditions. The paper also proposes novel evaluation methods, Wall Clock, Paused Clock, and Token Clock, to disentangle serving latency from a model's intrinsic temporal awareness.
items.figure_caption: Performance of Frontier Models on Realtime-Bench. Pass^3 measures the proportion of tasks successfully completed in all three independent trials, capturing consistency across repeated runs.

items.title: Shortcut Sensitivity in Agent-Safety Evaluations
items.abstract: This paper introduces a three-level framework to audit AI agent safety evaluations for "shortcut sensitivity," where evaluation data contains unintended cues that predict labels or influence agent decisions. The authors demonstrate that common evaluation methods can be unreliable, showing how simple cues like command length or exact tool matching can lead to inflated performance metrics. Their contribution lies in providing a rigorous method to identify and quantify these shortcuts, enabling more trustworthy safety evaluations.

items.summary: This repository optimizes AI coding agent context windows by sandboxing tool output, persisting session memory, and enforcing cross-platform routing through MCP and hooks.

items.summary: Ghidra is a powerful software reverse engineering framework that enables users to analyze and understand compiled code through features like decompilation, disassembly, and scripting.

papers.figure_caption: Overview. Ten agents discuss one fact for 16 rounds with k ∈ { 0 , 1 , 3 } k\( \in \)\{0,1,3\} adversarial agents pushing a false claim. Each round we measure both a benign agent’s public utterance and a private probe.

papers.title: CART: Compatible Routing for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
papers.abstract: This paper addresses catastrophic forgetting in multimodal instruction tuning by proposing Compatible Routing (CART). CART explicitly coordinates the adaptation of the visual projector and the language model by using task-specific experts for both modules. This joint adaptation, through weighted mixtures and inferred weights, aims to reduce representation drift and improve continual learning performance.

papers.title: Disagreement-Guided Weak-to-Strong Routing
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel method for "Disagreement-Guided Weak-to-Strong Routing" that avoids the need for costly ground-truth supervision. The core idea is to route a weak model's response to a stronger model based on the disagreement between multiple responses generated by the weak model itself. This disagreement signal serves as a proxy for correctness, enabling more efficient and reliable deployment of smaller models in resource-constrained environments.
papers.figure_caption: Corrected disagreement better approximates optimal routing than alternatives.

papers.title: Explaining the Roles of Experts in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs for Personalization
papers.abstract: This paper proposes personalizing Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs to address the challenges of understanding and controlling personalization in user-centric applications. By adapting MoE models and training crosscoders on their activations, the authors identify specific experts responsible for distinct personalization features. This approach enables more interpretable and localized personalization compared to dense LLMs, while maintaining competitive performance and reducing polysemanticity.

papers.title: Improving Environment-Agnostic Coding Agents: The Role of Scaffolding
papers.abstract: This paper investigates how to improve environment-agnostic coding agents without environment-specific engineering. The core method involves modifying agent instructions to encourage reporting difficulties and enabling automatic continuation, which demonstrably improves performance on some benchmarks. The contribution lies in showing that even with advanced models, strategic scaffolding focused on agent control and organization, rather than explicit knowledge, remains crucial for enhancing performance.

papers.title: OS-Helix: Unifying GUI Interaction and Code Execution in Native Computer-Using Agents
papers.abstract: OS-Helix is a multimodal agent that unifies GUI interaction and code execution by training end-to-end on hybrid data. Its core method involves creating realistic, executable desktop environments and generating grounded tasks to teach the agent how to seamlessly switch between visual and programmatic actions. This approach overcomes limitations of prompt-level tool composition, enabling more effective native computer-using agents.
papers.figure_caption: Overview of GUI-only, code-only, and hybrid computer use.

papers.title: PROBE: Learning to Audit Policy Compliance in Tool-Using LLM Agents
papers.abstract: This paper introduces PROBE, a method for training LLM-based auditors to detect policy violations in tool-using LLM agents. PROBE works by simulating realistic user interactions to uncover subtle, multi-turn policy breaches that traditional evaluation methods miss. Its core contribution is a novel approach to auditing agent compliance beyond just task completion or safety.

papers.title: Realtime-Bench: Can Frontier Models Solve Real-time Interactive Problems?
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Realtime-Bench, a new benchmark for evaluating large language models' ability to act in real-time interactive environments with strict temporal constraints. The benchmark reveals that current frontier models struggle significantly with these challenges, achieving low success rates even under ideal conditions. The paper also proposes novel evaluation methods, Wall Clock, Paused Clock, and Token Clock, to disentangle serving latency from a model's intrinsic temporal awareness.
papers.figure_caption: Performance of Frontier Models on Realtime-Bench. Pass^3 measures the proportion of tasks successfully completed in all three independent trials, capturing consistency across repeated runs.

papers.title: Shortcut Sensitivity in Agent-Safety Evaluations
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a three-level framework to audit AI agent safety evaluations for "shortcut sensitivity," where evaluation data contains unintended cues that predict labels or influence agent decisions. The authors demonstrate that common evaluation methods can be unreliable, showing how simple cues like command length or exact tool matching can lead to inflated performance metrics. Their contribution lies in providing a rigorous method to identify and quantify these shortcuts, enabling more trustworthy safety evaluations.
